with_skill.expectation: Response asks clarifying questions instead of delivering talking points, a message spine, or a prep brief.
Questions are asked one at a time rather than as a single list of ten or more questions.
The first question establishes the format: audio-only, video or livestream, and recorded-and-edited or live with no retakes.
Response drafts no message, claim, angle or sound bite before the format, episode length and host configuration, audience, and booked-topic questions are answered.
Response asks how many hours of prep the user has before the recording.
Response asks what the user is representing and what must be disclosed.
Response asks what outcome the user wants from the appearance.
Response describes the deliverable as one prep brief agreed section by section, not a finished document delivered in a single pass.
Response allocates the two available hours to the message spine and the opening answer only.
Response does not make show reconnaissance or listening to back-catalogue episodes the first task.
Response states that the disclosure line and the off-limits check are never traded away for time, whatever the prep ceiling.
Response attributes And-But-Therefore to Randy Olson rather than presenting it as generic storytelling advice.
Response asks the user to say each claim out loud, noting that a claim which is hard to say will not land under pressure.
Response names the flip-the-formula principle - start at the end - and attributes it to Brad Phillips.
Response applies the so-what test to the bio and states that years of experience earn nothing on their own.
Response states that the opening answer is the one moment of the episode the guest controls.
Response asks for or uses a concrete incident, system or number as the answer's opening material rather than a credential.
Response has the user say the answer aloud until it survives being clipped, rather than memorising it word for word.
Each candidate is in present tense and active voice.
Response states that the cold-read test, not the word count, is the real gate.
Response explains that the transcript and show notes become a machine-readable record later cited by AI assistants, which is why the number has to be spoken out loud.
Response states that bridging straight from the question is what a developer audience reads as PR training, and that it costs more trust than the awkward answer would have.
Response sorts ordinary questions from hostile ones and applies Answer, Detailed example, Describe relevance to the ordinary ones.
Response attributes the Answer-Detailed example-Describe relevance pattern to Matt Abrahams.
The eight predicted questions are drawn from the show's recurring threads, the booked topic, and the questions the user does not want to be asked.
Response flags that the licensing answer may need legal or employer sign-off before the recording.
Response removes the unpublished 3.2x internal benchmark rather than merely demoting it, on the grounds that only already-published numbers may be spoken and the recording outlives the embargo.
Each story carries something the user got wrong.
Response identifies a five-second moment for each story and attributes the idea to Matthew Dicks.
Response instructs opening each story at the opposite of its five-second moment.
Response recommends an up-down-up, Man in a Hole shape and credits the empirical test to Del Vecchio, Kharlamov, Parry and Pogrebna across 6,174 movie scripts.
Response notes the finding concerns the most talked-about films rather than the most liked.
Response plants one open loop early and closes it late, crediting the raise-questions-and-answer-them device to Ira Glass.
Response writes a one-sentence definition for each unavoidable piece of jargon.
Response sets a 15 to 20 second target for self-contained answers on a live show, attributed to broadcast media-training guidance.
Response covers the video dimension: clips get cut vertically, stay in frame, expect to be on camera while the hosts talk.
Response warns against opening a turn with agreement such as "I completely agree with what X just said".
Response names domination as the symmetrical failure and notes the camera is on everyone the whole time.
Response gives the one-sentence-answer drill: answer every likely question in exactly one sentence to find which points compress.
Response frames the panellist as the audience's advocate rather than the moderator's respondent.
Response has the user prepare a topic-avoidance plan naming which prepared message each avoided subject bridges to.
Response treats click attribution as a floor, never a total.
Response names repeat invitation, referral to another show, or an inbound speaking request as the real compounding return, despite being the slowest signal.
Response offers a branded-search and direct-traffic lift comparison over a 7 to 14 day window against baseline, labelled as directional only.
Response flags that the branded-search comparison is worthless if a launch overlapped the window.
Response states that the host controls distribution but has no incentive to relaunch an old episode.
Response distinguishes a topic from an angle and rejects "observability at scale" as an angle.
Response discards any candidate the show's back catalogue already covers twice, naming the OpenTelemetry migration episodes as the reason.
Response gives the reason for deleting rather than demoting: shortlisting a ruled-out shape makes the user rehearse an angle they cannot use.
Response ranks the angle shapes - war story, practical how-we-do-it, contrarian thesis - by audience moved per hour of preparation.
Response names the contrarian thesis as the highest-value and most expensive shape, and states the condition that promotes it.
Response notes that the contrarian thesis carries the highest compliance cost when it takes a public position against a named competitor or a standard.
Response treats the pre-interview call as the negotiation where the episode's content actually gets decided, not a formality.
Response discards any angle that is the user's own stock answer from the previous appearance.
Response caps the invited pitch at under 30 seconds.
Response states that claims about compliance, SLAs, pricing and roadmap can be quoted back in a procurement conversation.
Response requires every number spoken on air to be one the company already publishes.
Response gives one destination for the call to action, said slowly and spelled out if unusual.
